shared-harsanyi-derivative-cutoff-mvt.title: Complete shared proof: zero classical mixed partials and rectangular differences
shared-harsanyi-derivative-cutoff-mvt.overview: Globally zero classical mixed partials give zero rectangular differences. The actual coordinate-mask alternating sum is that difference; nonempty centering then recovers the original interaction.
assumptions: The original C1-function setting is retained. Global high-order mixed partials in 1-β are interpreted as classical existing derivatives; required prefix differentiability unfolds their definition and is not replaced by a total Lean deriv function returning zero.
All masks use the same fixed input baseline r and M∈ℕ. No analyticity, infinite Taylor representation, or polynomial premise is added.

definitions.body_md: Fix $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $v:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, x, and r. The coordinate mask keeps x_i on A and r_i elsewhere. Let $g(A)=v(x_A)$, $b=g(\varnothing)$, and $g_0(A)=g(A)-b$. The source interaction is $I(A)=I_{g_0}(A)$, with empty value zero. Let e_i be the coordinate unit vector and $a_i=x_i-r_i$ the actual masking increment.

proof_steps.title: Classical mixed partials and their existence order
proof_steps.body_md: The classical partial is $D_i f(z)=\left.\frac d{dt}f(z+t e_i)\right|_{t=0}$. Encode a multiindex by a nondecreasing coordinate list $(i_1,\ldots,i_q)$, and define $P_0=v$, $P_j=D_{i_j}P_{j-1}$. Classical existence of the stated mixed partials includes actual differentiability of each required prefix along the next coordinate, and 1-β gives $P_q\equiv0$. These existence conditions and the zero value are encoded together; only lists q>M are used. No extra global smoothness of all low derivatives is assumed. C1 alone does not imply existence of high derivatives. A fixed ascending order is used; a reverse convention can use the same difference argument in reverse order, without interchanging mixed partials.

proof_steps.title: Commutation of finite differences and true partial derivatives
proof_steps.body_md: Define $\delta_{a,i}f(z)=f(z+a e_i)-f(z)$. If f is differentiable along coordinate i everywhere, its finitely many translated sums and differences are too. Translation gives $D_i(f(\cdot+h))(z)=D_i f(z+h)$ because $(z+t e_i)+h=(z+h)+t e_i$. The one-variable difference rule yields $D_i(\delta_{a,j}f)=\delta_{a,j}(D_i f)$. Induction extends this to arbitrary finite rectangular differences. Only translations and finite additions are used, with no infinite series or higher directional chain rule.

proof_steps.title: Zero mixed partials imply zero rectangular differences
proof_steps.body_md: Induct on the direction-list length q, allowing arbitrary directions and real steps. For the empty list, both the difference and the order-zero partial are f, and its assumed zero value proves the claim. For a nonempty list, let R denote the remaining differences. The prefix-existence premise applies the induction hypothesis to $D_{i_1}f$, giving $R(D_{i_1}f)=0$. Commutation then gives $D_{i_1}(Rf)=0$. For fixed z, $H(t)=(Rf)(z+t e_{i_1})$ is differentiable on the whole real line with zero derivative. The mean value theorem gives $H(a_{i_1})=H(0)$, so the full rectangular difference is zero. Negative and zero steps require no new restrictions.

proof_steps.title: Bridge from rectangular differences to actual coordinate masks
proof_steps.body_md: List the distinct coordinates of S, take steps $a_i=x_i-r_i$, and start at r. Induct on that list. The empty difference is $v(r)=g(\varnothing)$. Adding a previously absent coordinate splits the rectangle into its translated and untranslated parts. On every remaining subset U, the translated vector is exactly the mask for $U\cup\{i\}$ and the untranslated vector is the mask for U. Subtracting the alternating sums is the insertion identity for $I_g(S)$. This bridge holds for an arbitrary model v; no polynomial representation is assumed.

proof_steps.title: Apply the original high-order multiindex condition
proof_steps.body_md: If $|S|\ge M+1$, list S in ascending order. The selected multiindex is 1 on S and 0 elsewhere, with total degree |S|>M. The original global 1-β supplies its classical derivative existence and zero value. The analytic lemma makes its rectangular difference zero, and the mask bridge gives $I_g(S)=0$. The step sizes only affect the difference, not derivative existence or its zero premise, so x and r are arbitrary.

proof_steps.title: Recover the original centered interaction and scope
proof_steps.body_md: Since |S|>M≥0, S is nonempty. Subtracting the constant baseline changes only the empty interaction, hence $I_{g_0}(S)=I_g(S)=0$, proving 1-α. Appendix B.2 uses Lemma 1’s infinite Taylor argument; this repair uses the original global 1-β in a finite-difference argument. The separate validity issue of a general Taylor-formula reading remains separate. A given valid Taylor representation gives another conditional grouping argument, whose proposition is not modified here.
